analysis.title: US Economic Outlook, 2026 Q3: Bond market selloff is no reason to panic
key_insights: Morningstar attributes the 2026 global bond selloff mainly to stronger perceived US economic and labor market strength, not fiscal worries. Nearly all of the yield increase is in real yields, and breakevens have barely moved since 2025.

The AI boom lifts aggregate demand and pushes up interest rates because GDP is already about at potential. Morningstar expects the AI boost to fade by 2028, either through steep job cuts or through an investment slowdown, and either case calls for deep Fed cuts.
Morningstar expects a net 100bp of rate cuts through end-2028 and a 10-year Treasury yield of 3.5% by 2029, from about 5.0% now.

Real wage growth turned negative at -0.4% y/y in Q2 2026, which supports corporate profits (over 13% of GDP vs 9% in 2019) but pushes household savings lower. Morningstar expects slower consumption as a result.
Q2 2026 headline GDP was 1.5% q/q annualized. Net exports and inventories subtracted 1.9pp, and final domestic demand rose 3.4%. Nonresidential fixed investment grew 8.5% annualized.
Morningstar expects exports and inventories to add an average 0.9pp to roughly 3% GDP growth in Q3 and Q4 2026, then growth to slow again.

GDP growth forecast: 2.3% in 2026, 2.1% in 2027, 1.7% in 2028, 2.5% in 2029 and 2.9% in 2030. Morningstar runs cooler than consensus, with unemployment averaging 4.6-4.7% in 2028 vs 4.2% for consensus.
Tech-related investment rose 14.1% y/y in H1 2026 and added about 1pp to GDP growth. Other nonresidential investment fell 3% and residential fell 4.7%.
Nonresidential investment is forecast at +6.1% in 2026, +4.2% in 2027 and +0.9% in 2028. Morningstar calls the 2027-28 slowdown a pause for monetization to catch up, not a bubble burst.

Productivity growth is running well above trend (1.9% average over 2020-25). Morningstar expects companies to trim headcount to earn a return on AI, pushing job growth to -0.3% in 2028 while GDP stays positive. The 2001-02 dot-com period is its analogue.
The labor market is slightly loose. Unemployment is 4.1% against a 3.7% natural rate, payroll growth is 0.4% y/y vs 0.35% breakeven, and the composite wage growth measure is 3.5% y/y.

White-collar services employment has fallen about 0.4% a year since 2024. The shortfall vs the 2017-19 trend is about 0.6 million jobs, probably mostly not AI. Unemployment for 23-25 year-old college grads is about 6%.
The personal saving rate was 2.8% in Q2 2026 vs 6.9% in 2018-19. Household net worth is about 600% of GDP vs 520% in 2018-19, which explains about 2pp of the 4pp saving shortfall.
PCE inflation is forecast at 3.4% in 2026 (2.6% in 2025), 2.4-2.5% in 2027 and about 2.0% on average over 2028-30. Oil adds about 0.8pp to 2026 PCE inflation, and tariffs still lift core goods.
Core PCE was 3.3% y/y in July. Air transport adds 0.2pp and core goods 0.5pp, partly from a software price measurement quirk that BEA will partly revise away.
Housing inflation is forecast to fall to 3.2% in 2026 and 3.0% in 2027, with market rents up only 1% y/y as of July 2026.

WTI was $102 on Sept. 14, up over 70% YTD, after the June US-Iran ceasefire failed to reopen the Strait of Hormuz and fighting restarted in August. Gasoline is up 90% YTD and diesel up 130%, helped by wide crack spreads.
Yields rose in 2026: 2-year from 3.47% to 4.64%, 10-year from 4.18% to 4.97%, 30-year from 4.84% to 5.33% (Dec 31 to Sept 11). The 30-year hit a 19-year high of 5.4% on Sept. 10.
The short end led the increase because expected fed funds for Q1 2027 moved 1.00-1.25pp higher. The 5y5y and 20y10y forwards rose 0.5pp and 0.4pp, which points to a higher expected terminal rate.
Gold's rise is not an inflation or debasement signal in Morningstar's view. The 30-year breakeven has stayed near 2.3% for five years, and Morningstar attributes gold buying more to momentum.

On the Kim-Wright model, the 2026 rise in the 10-year yield comes about equally from expected fed funds and term premium. Morningstar reads the term premium as reverting toward its 1990-2019 average of 1.0%, not as pricing fiscal crisis risk.

CBO projects federal debt rising from 98% of GDP at end-2025 to 175% by 2056, but that outlook is little changed since Feb 2024. Morningstar sees the term premium rising on excess supply of long-term debt, with AI capital demand a contributor.
Market pricing moved from 0.5pp of cuts expected through H1 2027 at the start of 2026 to 0.75pp of hikes now, with the terminal rate priced at the current range held indefinitely.
Morningstar expects two rate hikes through end-2026, then two cuts in H2 2027 and four in 2028. That puts fed funds at 2.50%-2.75% by end-2028, which it says is 175bp below market expectations.

Morningstar's rate forecasts (annual average): fed funds 3.66% in 2026, 4.04% in 2027, 3.23% in 2028, 2.60% in 2029-30. The 10-year is 4.60%, 4.50%, 3.80%, 3.50%, 3.50%. The 30-year mortgage is 6.55%, 6.45%, 5.65%, 5.25%, 5.25%.

risk_factors: AI investment slows sharply if monetization disappoints, cutting aggregate demand.
AI-driven productivity gains lead to steep job cuts, which have not yet occurred.
Household savings are low and real wages are negative, which could force a pullback in consumption.
Energy prices stay high if the Iran war and Hormuz disruption continue.
Sticky core inflation could keep the Fed hiking.
Rising federal debt (98% of GDP to 175% by 2056) adds to term premium via supply of long-term debt.
The term premium is a latent variable estimated from a model, so the decomposition is uncertain.

tension_points.bull_case: Morningstar argues the selloff reflects economic strength: real yields drove the rise, breakevens are flat, and the short end led as rate-cut expectations were repriced. This is not a fiscal crisis.
tension_points.bear_case: The common view blames US fiscal health. Morningstar concedes debt supply raises the term premium and the 30-year/5-year spread has widened by over 0.5pp since October 2023.
tension_points.what_invalidates: A rise in breakeven inflation or term premium unconnected to growth data would point to fiscal or debasement fears.

tension_points.bull_case: Morningstar expects two hikes in 2026, then cuts to 2.50%-2.75% by end-2028 as core inflation eases and growth weakens.
tension_points.bear_case: The market prices 0.75pp of hikes and holds the 4.25%-4.50% range indefinitely, on sticky core inflation and AI-supported demand.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Steep AI-driven job cuts or a sharp AI investment slowdown would weaken demand and force the Fed to cut deeply.

theme_stances.key_argument: Shifting perceptions of US economic and labor market strength have played a bigger role than fiscal worries in the 2026 yield rise.
theme_stances.evidence: shifting perceptions of the strength of the US economy and labor market

theme_stances.key_argument: AI investment and the stock wealth effect raise aggregate demand and rates, and that effect should fade by 2028.
theme_stances.evidence: Currently, AI is only boosting aggregate demand, putting upward pressure on interest rates.

theme_stances.key_argument: Flat long-run breakevens contradict the currency debasement explanation for gold's rise.
theme_stances.evidence: investors were snapping up gold more because of price momentum
